title: Ganesh Chaturthi: the moon that laughed
hookLine: the moon laughs at Ganesha's fall, and the clay goes back to the water
carry: god has a form, and is beyond it
tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
last: THE AVATAR COMES IN THE DARKEST HOUR.

cards: Ganesh Chaturthi night, late summer. The drums have finally gone quiet. Your family's clay Ganesha is home on a little throne, with lamps, flowers and a plate of modaks, the sweet dumplings he loves.
You step outside for air, and an aunt grabs your arm. Don't look up. Not tonight.
Don't look at the moon. It sounds like a superstition. It's really the end of a story: a god who fell off his ride, and the one who laughed at him.

teach.h: THE MOUSE, THE SNAKE, THE SPILLED SWEETS.
teach.b: Here's the story as families tell it. It's Ganesha's birthday, and everyone has been feeding him modaks. Belly full, he rides home at night on his mouse.
A snake slides across the path, the mouse panics, Ganesha tumbles off, and the sweets spill everywhere. He gets up, gathers them, and ties the snake around his middle as a belt.
And up in the sky the moon, proud of his own beauty, laughs at the round god in the dust. Ganesha curses him: no one will want to look at you.

teach.h: THE MOON SAW ONLY A SHAPE.
teach.b: The moon goes dark and begs, the gods plead, and Ganesha softens it: only on this one night, whoever looks at the moon will be wrongly blamed for something.

The tellings say even Krishna glimpsed the moon that night and was accused of stealing a well-known jewel, the Syamantaka, and had to clear his own name. So on Ganesh Chaturthi, many families keep their eyes off the moon.
Now the teaching. Many teachers read the story this way: the moon laughed at a shape, the elephant head, the belly, the snake belt. He saw only the form.
Hinduism has two words for this.
Saguna: God with form and qualities, a face you can see, feed and love.

teach.h: GOD HAS A FORM, AND IS BEYOND IT.
teach.b: Nirguna: God beyond every form. Many Hindus hold both, and the festival acts it out. For days, families love Ganesha in clay, the saguna way, with lamps and modaks.
Then they carry him to the water and let the clay go, because he was never only the clay. The crowds shout Ganpati Bappa Morya, and in Marathi, come back soon next year. The form goes.
The god doesn't. It's why a Hindu home can hold many pictures of God, and still say God is one, beyond them all.

how: For Ganesh Chaturthi, Hindu families and neighborhoods install clay images of Ganesha at home or in public pandals, worship him with lamps, flowers, durva grass and modaks for one and a half to ten days, then immerse the image in water in a joyful procession; many avoid looking at the moon on the festival night, and many now choose unpainted clay. The great public festivals grew from Pune in the 1890s, with Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

games.q: what's inside the festival — tap the pairs.
p: God with form, to see and love

s: on Ganesh Chaturthi night, many families avoid looking at the moon
in the story the moon laughed at Ganesha, and the curse falls on this one night.
families put Ganesha in the water because they're done with him
they loved him in clay, and he was never only the clay: God beyond form, nirguna.
Ganesh Chaturthi falls on the fourth day of the moon's bright half

games.q: the festival's last day. your little cousin is crying: 'if we put Ganesha in the lake, is he gone?' what do you say?
o: yes, until we buy a new one next year.
no. we loved him in clay, but he was never only the clay.
let's just keep him on the shelf instead.
games.why: saguna and nirguna: God with a face you can love, and beyond every face. the clay goes back to the water; the god doesn't leave.

practice: If you pray, look at a picture or murti of Ganesha, or any face of God you love, for one slow minute: the eyes, the hands, the small details. Say his name, or Om Gam Ganapataye Namah.
Then close your eyes, let the picture fade, and stay with what's still there. If you don't pray, do it with a photo of someone you love. The picture goes.

wordCard.voice: Ganesh Chaturthi. The fourth day of the bright moon, when Ganesha comes home in clay, families keep their eyes off the moon, and the clay goes back to the water.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Ganesha + chaturthi (the fourth day of a lunar fortnight).

carryVoice: Your line: god has a form, and is beyond it. The moon only saw the shape. Seventy-nine days, and counting.
